design_detail: Single-arm pilot with a baseline interview and a follow-up visit at least two weeks later (described in the abstract as a one-month follow-up), filed as a prospective cohort. Young adults aged 18–35 in Rhode Island who reported heroin use, cocaine use, injection, or buying prescription pills on the street in the past 30 days were recruited May to September 2017. Everyone received a baseline interview, a video-based training, ten single-use BTNX fentanyl urine test strips (maker's detection level 20 ng/ml) with written instructions, overdose education and a 4 mg intranasal naloxone kit. The testing method was allocated by enrolment order, not at random: the first 40 enrolled were told to test their urine after use (post-consumption), the rest drug residue or a dissolved drug sample before use (pre-consumption). Outcomes at follow-up were self-reported strip use, positive results, actions after a positive result and acceptability; comparisons are unadjusted bivariable tests between participants who used a strip and those who used none, and between participants who did and did not report a positive result. Read with ROBINS-I rather than the JBI prevalence checklist because receiving strips with training is an intervention and the paper compares groups and infers behaviour change. Read from the PubMed Central author manuscript, which has no journal pagination; ‘AM p.’ gives the PDF page.
can_establish: How many young adults who use drugs in Rhode Island in 2017, given ten fentanyl test strips with training and naloxone, said within about a month that they had used a strip, how many reported a positive result, what they said they did after it, and how acceptable they found the strips.
cannot_establish: Whether being given or using strips, or receiving a positive result, changes overdose risk behaviour or overdose (no group without strips, unverified self-reports, unadjusted and confounded comparisons, an outcome defined only after a positive result), nor how accurate the strips were in participants' hands, nor whether testing urine after use and testing drugs before use differ.

sample.recruitment: Advertisement and community: bus and online advertisements, fliers and word of mouth in Rhode Island, May to September 2017, plus four people from an earlier study of young adults' non-medical prescription opioid use (RAPIDS) who had agreed to be recontacted (Methods 2.1, 1st paragraph, AM p. 3). Paid US$25 for the first visit and US$50 for the second (Methods 2.1, 4th paragraph, AM p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18–35, living in Rhode Island, and self-reported heroin use, cocaine use, injection drug use or buying prescription pills on the street in the past 30 days (AM p. 3). No exclusion criteria are stated. Two people who returned were excluded from analysis for missing information (AM p. 5).
sample.demographics: Analytic sample (Table 1, AM p. 13–14; Results, 2nd paragraph, AM p. 6–7): mean age 26.5 years (SD 4.7); 45 male (56%), 33 female (41%), 3 transgender or other (4%); 44 White (54%), 37 non-white (46%); 19 Hispanic or Latino (24%); 73 (90%) with a high-school diploma or more; 48 (59%) ever homeless; weekly use of heroin 27 (33%), cocaine 31 (38%) and non-medical prescription pills 17 (21%); ever injected 42 (52%); ever dealt drugs 63 (78%); ever overdosed 29 (36%); ever witnessed an overdose 50 (62%). At baseline 55 (68%) agreed they were concerned about their own drugs being contaminated with fentanyl (Table 2, AM p. 15).
sample.attrition: 83 of 93 (89.2%) returned and 81 (87%) were analysed. The authors state that those who returned and those lost did not differ demographically or behaviourally, with results not shown (Results, 1st paragraph, AM p. 6). By group (editors' calculation from the allocation rule and the analysed numbers): 34 of the 40 assigned to urine testing and 47 of the 53 assigned to drug-sample testing were analysed. Item-level missing data in Tables 1–2 (table footnote, AM p. 16).
sample.selection_effects: A paid convenience sample recruited by advertisement, in a state the authors describe as severely affected by fentanyl; people willing to attend two research visits and be trained may be more cautious, better informed or more connected to services than other young people who use drugs. The two testing groups were formed by enrolment order and differed at baseline (weekly cocaine use 49% in the drug-sample group v 24% in the urine group, p = .022). The comparison groups (strip used or not; positive result or not) were formed after baseline by participants' own behaviour and drug supply, and the positive-result group differed sharply in weekly heroin use, injection and witnessing overdose (Table 1).

exposure.measurement: Intervention (Methods 2.1, 2nd–4th paragraphs, AM p. 4–5): a training video on testing urine or drugs (by assigned method) and a second on reading results, a strip to examine, ten single-use BTNX rapid fentanyl urine strips for personal use, written and graphic instructions, and a sticker on each strip showing a positive (‘fentanyl’) and a negative (‘unknown’) result; overdose education and naloxone distribution with a 4 mg intranasal naloxone kit, delivered by trained research staff. Participants were told that fentanyl or analogues could be present despite a negative strip and to practise overdose prevention whatever the result (AM p. 4–5). Strip use, the number used and the number positive were self-reported at follow-up and not verified (Discussion, 5th paragraph, AM p. 9).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (no drug was given). Strips: detection level 20 ng/ml as stated by the maker (AM p. 3). Participants used a median of 3 strips (IQR 1–6; the denominator is not stated) and 10 (12%) used all ten (Results, 3rd paragraph, AM p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Weekly use of heroin (33%), cocaine (38%) and non-medical prescription pills (21%) was recorded at baseline (Table 1); polysubstance use was not otherwise measured or analysed. Which drug each strip was used on, and whether urine positives reflected intended fentanyl use, are not reported.

comparison.controls: No group without strips: everyone received strips, training, overdose education and naloxone. Internal comparisons only: participants who used at least one strip (62) v none (19), and, among those who used a strip, those reporting at least one positive result (31) v none (31). The urine (34) and drug-sample (47) groups were allocated by enrolment order.
comparison.matching: None, and no adjustment; the authors say the sample was too small for multivariable analysis (Discussion, 5th paragraph, AM p. 9).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The baseline ‘behaviour’ was the reported response to the last drug the participant was confident contained fentanyl, or, for those unsure, a hypothetical intention (Methods 2.2, 3rd paragraph, AM p. 5), so baseline and follow-up answers measure different things. Not measured: fentanyl in each participant's supply, which drug was tested and when, use of other harm-reduction services, and changes in the drug supply over the May–September recruitment, which the enrolment-order allocation confounds with testing method.

outcomes.instruments: Interviewer-administered surveys at baseline and follow-up written for the study (not reproduced; training protocol and other materials available on request, AM p. 4). Primary outcomes: any strip used (yes or no) and, among those who used one, at least one positive result (yes or no). Secondary: ‘any positive overdose risk behavior change related to a fentanyl test result’, defined as no risk-reduction practice at baseline but at least one after a positive result, from the options Did a tester, Went slower, Threw them out, Used less and Used with someone else around. Acceptability: items including confidence in reading results, ease of continuing and wanting to use strips in future, on a 4-point agreement scale, and preferred places to obtain strips (Methods 2.2, AM p. 5–6).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated instruments. Self-report, with social desirability and recall bias acknowledged by the authors (AM p. 9).
outcomes.operationalization: Uptake = any strip used; positive = any self-reported positive strip, from urine or drug; behaviour change = a risk-reduction answer after a positive result where none was given at baseline. Agreement answers were collapsed to ‘agree’ v ‘disagree/neutral’, with ‘do not know’ and refusals counted as disagree/neutral (AM p. 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six outcomes were tested (two primary, one secondary and the three acceptability items in Table 3), with Pearson chi-square, Wilcoxon rank-sum and Fisher's exact tests, two-sided at 0.05 (Methods 2.3, AM p. 6). Tables 1–3 print 49 bivariable p-values (editors' count), 13 of them below 0.05, and the text adds one more (cocaine use by testing group).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: outcomes are self-reports given in interviews with research staff; no blinding is described.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals are printed, only percentages and p-values. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% CI): any strip used 62/81 = 76.5% (66.2–84.4%); at least one positive among those who used a strip 31/62 = 50.0% (37.9–62.1%); would like to use strips in future 77/81 = 95.1% (88.0–98.1%); continuing would be easy 75/81 = 92.6% (84.8–96.6%). Behaviour-change composite (Table 3): 21/31 (67.7%; 50.1–81.4%) with a positive result v 4/31 (12.9%; 5.1–28.9%) without, difference 54.8 points (Newcombe 95% CI 31.1–70.6), printed p < .001; participants who used a strip v none 25/62 (40.3%) v 6/19 (31.6%), difference 8.7 points (Newcombe −16.4 to 29.2), printed p = .513.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned; approved by the Brown University IRB as a pilot of feasibility to inform a larger trial of efficacy (Methods 2.1, 1st paragraph, AM p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Several results are ‘not shown’: the comparison of those who returned with those lost, positive results by testing method, and other differences between testing groups (AM p. 6–7). The frequency of ‘Took them anyways’ after a positive result is not reported, though it was a response option (AM p. 6–7). Uptake by testing method is not reported, although the Discussion says uptake was high whichever method was assigned (AM p. 8). The denominator of the 58% who gave strips to others is not stated.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; a pilot with 81 analysed and 31 positive results; the authors note the sample was too small for multivariable analysis (AM p. 9).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In about a month, 62 of 81 analysed participants (77%) reported using at least one of ten strips (median 3), and half of them (31) reported at least one positive result, unverified, from urine after use or from drugs before use. Of the 31, 45% said they used smaller amounts, 42% went slower, 39% used with someone else around and 36% did a tester; about one in ten threw the drugs out or sold them; how many used them anyway is not reported. A behaviour-change composite was more frequent with a positive result (21 of 31 v 4 of 31) but not detectably more frequent in participants who used a strip than in those who used none (40% v 32%, p = .513), and six people who used no strip are counted as having changed behaviour in response to a test result. Acceptability was high (95% wanted to use strips again).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports that a positive result was “significantly associated with reporting a positive change in overdose risk behavior” (AM p. 2), and the Discussion calls this “preliminary evidence that fentanyl test strips could promote engagement in risk reduction practices” that may reduce overdose (AM p. 9). The comparison is unadjusted and confounded (weekly heroin use 65% v 10%, ever injected 81% v 26%), the outcome by its definition can occur only after a positive result, and the one comparison not built on that definition (strip used or not) shows no clear difference. The Conclusions call the strips “a feasible and acceptable harm reduction tool to detect IMF presence in illicit drugs” (AM p. 9), but no result was verified and 34 of the 81 were assigned to test urine after use, which shows exposure rather than drug content. The uptake and acceptability statements match the descriptive results, and the limitations paragraph is candid.

timeline.event: Pilot data collected in Rhode Island, May to September.

Krieger et al. (2018), Harm Reduction Journal: baseline results of the same pilot, reporting high willingness to use strips; cited, not read. It would need its own reference id (this card holds krieger_2018).

Tupper et al. (2018) and Lysyshyn et al. (2017), cited as evaluating strip uptake and behavioural outcomes in Canadian supervised consumption settings, and McGowan et al. (2018) on fentanyl self-testing outside supervised settings; not read.
This study published (November issue; author manuscript in PubMed Central).

Green et al. (2020): two-site laboratory validation of BTNX strips on police-seized samples; its site values (sensitivity 100.0% and 96.3%, specificity 98.1% and 90.4%, card sc_green_2020) match on rounding the figures this paper cites from a 2018 Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health web report.
Bergh et al. (2021): laboratory study of four urine strip brands, including the BTNX strip used here, against 28 fentanyl analogues and other drugs (card sc_bergh_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: No replication of the behaviour-change finding appears in the sources read for this card (the paper and the project's exemplar cards); later studies were not searched by this reader, so the status is provisional. The authors themselves present the association as preliminary and call for a larger efficacy study (AM p. 9).

funding.funder: A research seed grant from the Office of the Vice President of Research at Brown University to Brandon D.L. Marshall; the funders had no role in study design, data analysis or the decision to publish (Role of Funding Source, AM p. 10).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (AM p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Brown University (Epidemiology; Emergency Medicine), the University of British Columbia, the British Columbia Centre for Disease Control, Vancouver Coastal Health, Boston University School of Medicine and Boston Medical Center (Grayken Center for Addiction) and the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health; the strip-accuracy figures the paper cites come from a Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health report. The strips were bought from BTNX; no support from the maker is mentioned. The first author helped run the surveys, drafted the paper and ran the analyses; the senior author conceived the pilot (Author Contributions, AM p. 1). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial among people who use drugs comparing strip distribution with training against the same overdose education and naloxone without strips, with strip results verified (for example photographed strips, or laboratory confirmation of a share of samples), the same prospective behaviour questions in both arms at fixed times, and overdose outcomes, large and long enough to detect a difference.

domains.note: No group went without strips. The positive-result comparison is unadjusted: those with a positive result used heroin weekly far more often (65% v 10%), had more often injected (81% v 26%) and witnessed an overdose (94% v 29%), and were older and more often homeless; receiving a positive result depends on the same drug-use pattern that shapes the baseline answers defining ‘change’.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Paid convenience sample recruited by advertisement; the groups compared are formed after the start of the intervention by participants' own behaviour (using strips) and supply (fentanyl present); analysis restricted to the 81 of 93 with follow-up and complete data.
Strip use, number used and results were self-reported at follow-up and not verified (authors); urine and drug-sample tests are pooled; 58% gave strips to others, so who tested what is uncertain.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Everyone also received overdose education and naloxone and was told to practise overdose prevention whatever the result, a co-intervention shared by all; testing method allocated by enrolment order; adherence (median 3 of 10 strips) self-reported.
12 of 93 (13%) not analysed; the authors say those lost did not differ but show no data; item-level missing data in Tables 1–2; some percentages in the text cannot be formed from 31 respondents.

Self-reported behaviour in interviews with research staff (social desirability and recall, as the authors say); ‘change’ compares answers about the last suspected exposure or a hypothetical intention at baseline with reported behaviour after a positive result at follow-up; the outcome can be measured only in people who found fentanyl, so it is not comparable across the groups compared, yet Table 3 assigns it to 6 people who used no strip.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol or registration; the composite is defined differently in the Methods and in the footnote to Table 3 (which adds ‘Took them anyways’); about 50 unadjusted tests; several analyses ‘not shown’; the frequency of ‘Took them anyways’ is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because strips with training are an intervention and the paper infers behaviour change from internal comparisons (topic instruction; METHODS §5.3). As evidence that a positive strip result, or using strips, changes overdose risk behaviour, the study is at critical risk of bias: no group went without strips, the positive-result comparison is unadjusted and confounded by heroin use and injection, and the outcome is self-reported, defined only for people who found fentanyl and yet assigned to people who used no strip. Citable for: uptake within about a month (62 of 81 used at least one strip), self-reported positive results (31 of 62, unverified), the actions participants said they took after a positive result, acceptability, and the sharing of strips with others, all as self-reports from one paid convenience sample of young adults in Rhode Island in 2017. Not citable for: effects on behaviour or overdose, strip accuracy, or a comparison of urine testing after use with drug testing before use.

key_findings.finding: Pilot in Rhode Island, May to September 2017: 93 young adults aged 18–35 completed baseline, 83 (89.2%) returned for follow-up and 81 (87%) with complete outcome data were analysed, 34 told to test urine after use and 47 told to test drug residue or a dissolved sample before use. Testing method was allocated by enrolment order (the first 40 to urine testing).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods 2.1, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: At baseline every participant received a training video on use and on reading results, ten single-use BTNX fentanyl urine strips (maker's detection level 20 ng/ml) with written instructions, overdose education and a 4 mg intranasal naloxone kit, and was told that a negative strip does not exclude fentanyl. Visits were paid US$25 and US$50.

The paper cites a two-site study reporting BTNX strip sensitivity of 96 and 100% and specificity of 90 and 98% against laboratory methods, with detection of acetylfentanyl and furanylfentanyl, and notes that the strips show presence or absence, not amount.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2.1, 1st paragraph (begins AM p. 3; figures on AM p. 4)
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from a 2018 web report; they match the site values of Green et al. (2020), card sc_green_2020.

key_findings.finding: Analytic sample: mean age 26.5 (SD 4.7); 56% male; 46% non-white; 59% ever homeless; weekly heroin use 33%; ever injected 52%; ever overdosed 36%; ever witnessed an overdose 62%; 68% concerned about their own drugs being contaminated with fentanyl. Weekly cocaine use was more common in the drug-sample group than the urine group (49% v 24%, p = .022).

Uptake: 62 of 81 (77%) reported using at least one strip; median 3 strips used (IQR 1–6; denominator not stated); 10 (12%: 4 drug-sample, 6 urine) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated). Participants who used a strip more often reported ever having dealt drugs (52 of 62, 84%, v 11 of 19, 58%; p = .038); no other baseline characteristic or attitude differed significantly.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (Lifetime History of Drug Dealing); Table 2

key_findings.finding: 31 of the 62 who used a strip (50%) reported at least one positive result (self-reported, not verified); positives did not differ by testing method (results not shown). Those with a positive result were older (mean 27.5 v 24.9, p = .030) and more often had been homeless (71% v 45%, p = .040), used heroin weekly (65% v 10%), had ever injected (81% v 26%) and had ever witnessed an overdose (94% v 29%) (each p < .001).

At baseline, more of those who later reported a positive result had been concerned about friends using fentanyl-contaminated drugs (30 of 31, 97%, v 65%; p = .001), about friends overdosing (31 of 31 v 52%; p < .001) and about overdosing themselves (71% v 29%; p = .001), had ever used a drug they were confident contained fentanyl (84% v 16%; p < .001) and had ever overdosed on one they thought might (32% v 6%; p = .022). Concern about their own drugs being contaminated: 84% v 52%, printed p = .088.
key_findings.note: Table 2 prints 31 (31) for the friends-overdosing cell (31 of 31 is 100%). From the printed counts the own-drugs row gives p of about 0.01 (Pearson chi-square 0.007, Fisher 0.013; editors' calculation), not .088.

key_findings.finding: Of the 31 with a positive result: 45% used smaller amounts, 42% went slower, 39% used with someone else around, 36% did a tester, 10% threw the drugs out, 10% sold them and 7% gave them away (more than one answer allowed). How many used the drugs anyway is not reported.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 45%, 42%, 39% and 10% fit 14, 13, 12 and 3 of 31, but 36% and 7% cannot be formed from 31 (11/31 = 35.5%, 2/31 = 6.5%), so some items had fewer answers, unexplained.

key_findings.finding: Behaviour-change composite (‘any positive overdose risk behavior change related to a fentanyl test result’): 21 of 31 (68%) with a positive result v 4 of 31 without (printed 32%), p < .001; participants who used a strip v none 25 of 62 (40%) v 6 of 19 (32%), p = .513; overall 31 of 81 (38%).
key_findings.note: 4 of 31 is 12.9% and the matching ‘No’ cell 27 of 31 is 87.1%, printed 68% (editors' calculation). By the Methods definition the outcome requires a positive result, yet 6 people who used no strip and 4 with no positive result are counted; the footnote to Table 3 also lists ‘Took them anyways’ in the composite.

key_findings.finding: A greater proportion of the drug-sample (pre-consumption) group than of the urine (post-consumption) group is said to have reported a positive behaviour change after a positive result (62% v 38%); no denominators or test are given.
key_findings.note: The two figures sum to 100% and both lie below the overall 21 of 31 (68%) among those with a positive result, which within-group proportions cannot do; they fit 13 and 8 of the 21 who changed (editors' calculation), a split of the changers rather than a comparison of rates.

key_findings.finding: At follow-up 79 (98%) reported confidence in their ability to use the strips, 77 (95%) wanted to use them in future and 75 (93%) said continuing would be easy; wanting to use them in future was more common among those who had used a strip (61 of 62 v 16 of 19, p = 0.041). Places participants would be comfortable getting strips: community health clinics 72%, community-based organizations 57%, pharmacies 52%, health department offices 52%, syringe services programmes 49%, online stores 44%.
key_findings.note: Confidence in reading results is given as 62 (77%) in the text (AM p. 8) and in the Table 3 overall column, but the Table 3 subgroup cells add to 78 agreeing (59 + 19) and 3 disagreeing (editors' calculation); the 79 (98%) for using the strips appears in no table.

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: self-reports subject to social desirability and recall bias; strip results not verified; a convenience sample of young adults in New England, where fentanyl is prevalent; a sample too small for multivariable analysis; strip accuracy on drug samples tested by people who use drugs not assessed; reasons for not using strips (23%) not asked.

The authors conclude that young adults reported high uptake and acceptability and that the strips are a feasible and acceptable harm-reduction tool; they describe the association between a positive result and behaviour change as preliminary evidence and call for a larger study of effects on overdose and risk behaviour.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 counts behaviour change ‘related to a fentanyl test result’ in 6 of 19 participants who used no strip and in 4 of 31 who used strips but had no positive result, although the Methods define the outcome as change after receiving a positive result.
reporting_issues.consequence: The composite is not what the Methods describe, so the reported association with a positive result cannot be interpreted; cite the actions after a positive result descriptively instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list the risk-reduction answers as Did a tester, Went slower, Threw them out, Used less and Used with someone else around, with ‘Took them anyways’ among the other answers; the footnote to Table 3 includes ‘Took them anyways’ in the composite.
reporting_issues.consequence: If it was included, the ‘positive’ composite counts using the drugs anyway as risk reduction.

reporting_issues.issue: Misprinted percentages: in Table 3 the no-positive column shows 4 (32) and 27 (68), in Table 1 lifetime overdose shows 17 (5), and in Table 2 friends overdosing shows 31 (31); the Table 3 header reads %(n) while the cells give n (%), and in two Table 2 rows the positive and no-positive columns add to 62 while their parent column totals 60. By editors' calculation the four percentages should be 12.9, 87.1, 55 and 100.

Confidence figures disagree: the abstract and text give 79 (98%) confident in using the strips, an item in no table; the text and Table 3 give 62 (77%) confident in reading results overall, but the Table 3 subgroup cells show 59 and 19 agreeing and 3 and 0 disagreeing, which by editors' calculation add to 78 and 3, not 62 and 19.
reporting_issues.consequence: Confidence in reading results is uncertain (77% or about 96%); the 62 (77%) may have been copied from the number who used a strip, which is also 62 (77%).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints p = .088 for concern about one's own drugs being contaminated by positive result, but by editors' calculation its counts (26 of 31 v 16 of 31) give p of about 0.01 by chi-square or Fisher's test. Other printed p-values do not reproduce from the counts either (race by positive result .206 printed, 0.30 by chi-square; lifetime overdose by strip use .482 printed, 0.32).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a count or a p-value is wrong; the abstract's list of baseline concerns associated with a positive result cannot be checked, and table p-values should not be cited without the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that almost all participants with a positive result had been concerned about overdosing themselves and that a majority had overdosed on a drug they thought contained fentanyl; Table 2 gives 22 of 31 (71%) and 10 of 31 (32%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text overstates two baseline differences; cite Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Among the 31 with a positive result, 36% did a tester and 7% gave the drugs away; neither percentage can be formed from 31 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Unexplained missing answers; the denominators of the reported actions are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The 62% v 38% pre- v post-consumption behaviour-change contrast cannot be two within-group rates (both lie below the overall 68% among those with a positive result); by editors' calculation it fits the split of the 21 who changed (13 and 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: Not evidence that testing drugs before use produced more change than testing urine after use.

reporting_issues.issue: The behaviour-change association is given as p ≤ 0.01 in the abstract, p ≤ .001 in the text and < .001 in Table 3.

verification.source_read: PDF of the PubMed Central author manuscript (HHS Public Access, 17 pages without journal pagination, cited as AM p. = PDF page; published in final form in International Journal of Drug Policy 2018;61:52–58), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Fentanyl-and-analogues/Krieger_2018_RapidFentanylTestStrips.pdf: all text, Tables 1–3 (AM pp. 13–17, rendered and every cell checked against the text extraction; totals and p-values recomputed), author contributions, conflict-of-interest and funding statements, reference list. No supplementary material is mentioned; the questionnaire and training materials are available only on request.
